The permissions granted to an entity by multiple permissions types\\\\nare more complex. For more details about how AWS evaluates policies, see Policy evaluation logic.\\\\n\\\\n**Identity-based policies with boundaries** \u2013\\\\nIdentity-based policies are inline or managed policies that are attached to a user,\\\\ngroup of users, or role. Identity-based policies grant permission to the entity, and\\\\npermissions boundaries limit those permissions. The effective permissions are the\\\\nintersection of both policy types. An explicit deny in either of these policies\\\\noverrides the allow.\\\\n\\\\n**Resource-based policies** \u2013 Resource-based\\\\npolicies control how the specified principal can access the resource to which the\\\\npolicy is attached.\\\\n\\\\n*Resource-based policies for IAM users*\\\\n: Within the same account, resource-based policies that grant permissions to\\\\n an IAM user ARN (that is not an AWS STS federated user principal session)\\\\n are not limited by an implicit deny in an identity-based policy or\\\\n permissions boundary.\\\\n\\\\n*Resource-based policies for IAM roles*\\\\n: **IAM role** \u2013 Resource-based\\\\n policies that grant permissions to an IAM role ARN are limited by an\\\\n implicit deny in a permissions boundary or session policy.\\\\n\\\\n **IAM role session** \u2013 Within the\\\\n same account, resource-based policies that grant permissions to an IAM\\\\n role session ARN grant permissions directly to the assumed role session.\\\\n Permissions granted directly to a session are not limited by an implicit\\\\n deny in an identity-based policy, a permissions boundary, or session policy.\\\\n When you assume a role and make a request, the principal making the request\\\\n is the IAM role session ARN and not the ARN of the role itself.\\\\n\\\\n*Resource-based policies for AWS STS federated user principal\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How can I resolve access denied issues caused by permissions boundaries?\",\"context\":\"Short description\\\\n-----------------\\\\n\\\\nAWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) returns access denied or unauthorized errors when your policy doesn\\'t meet specific condition requirements.\\\\n\\\\nTo resolve the issue, identify the specific IAM user or IAM role that causes the problem. {"id": "d868a85b-f3d9-4cfa-8ab2-9957a9876c80", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Here's the order I'd walk, from broadest to narrowest — because any explicit **Deny** at any layer wins immediately, regardless of what's below it:

**1. Explicit Deny check (short-circuits everything)**
Before anything else, any single explicit `Deny` in *any* of the policies below overrides every `Allow`, no matter where it lives. So in practice I scan all layers first just for denies.

**2. Organization-level policies**
- **SCPs** (Service Control Policies) — org/OU-wide guardrails, commonly used to block specific Bedrock model IDs or SageMaker actions account-wide
- **RCPs** (Resource Control Policies) — newer org-wide guardrails that restrict what resource policies can grant

**3. Resource-based policies**
- Bedrock resource policies (e.g., on AgentCore resources, knowledge bases, agents)
- KMS key policies (if the model, endpoint, or data is encrypted)
- S3 bucket policies (training data, model artifacts)
- VPC endpoint policies (if calling via PrivateLink)

**4. Identity-based policies**
The IAM user/role's attached managed + inline policies — this is where most `bedrock:InvokeModel`, `sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint`, etc. permissions actually get granted.

**5. Permissions boundary**
If the role/user has one attached, effective permissions are the *intersection* of the identity policy and the boundary — the boundary can't grant, only cap.

**6. Session policies**
If the caller assumed a role via STS with an inline session policy, that's the last filter applied to the assumed session.

**7. Service-specific gates (not IAM, but often the real culprit for AI/ML)**
- **Bedrock model access** — you can have perfect IAM permissions and still get denied if the account hasn't been granted access to that specific foundation model
- **SageMaker execution role** — distinct from the caller's IAM identity; the endpoint/training job runs under its own role, which needs its own S3/KMS/ECR permissions

One useful recent change: AWS access-denied error messages now include the actual **ARN of the specific policy** (SCP, RCP, identity policy, session policy, or boundary) that caused the denial, which cuts out a lot of this manual walk if the error message is recent enough to carry it.

Want me to pull the actual error and the caller's policies to see where it's failing?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
